title: Contact on Ktaadn
hookLine: on Mount Katahdin, Thoreau is shaken by raw matter: contact, contact! (The Maine Woods)

lines: ON THE WAY DOWN, IT BREAKS OPEN.
cards: Cloud, all the way down to the rocks. Thoreau is climbing a mountain in Maine, the one he spells Ktaadn and maps now call Katahdin.
Near the top he's alone in a gray fog so thick he can barely see the boulders under his hands. No view, no reward. He turns back.
And on the way down, crossing bare, burned-over ground, something breaks open in him. The calm writer of the pond starts piling up exclamation marks, as if the sentences can't hold what he's feeling.

teach.b: First, the ground. It isn't a park or a farm or a pretty view. He calls it no man's garden: earth nobody planted, nobody tidied, nobody owns.
Matter that owes him nothing. Second, a strange reversal. He admits his own body has become strange to him.
He isn't afraid of spirits, he says; what unsettles him is bodies, solid things.

teach.h: THE PLAIN ROCK AS THE MYSTERY.
teach.b: For a man who wrote so much about spirit, it's a startling turn: the ghostly felt familiar, and the plain rock felt like the mystery. Third, the outburst. The real mystery, he says, isn't some far-off spirit world.

teach.h: ROCKS, TREES, WIND ON OUR CHEEKS.
teach.b: It's ordinary life in nature, being shown matter and touching it: "rocks, trees, wind on our cheeks!"
Then four short cries: "Contact! Contact! Who are we? where are we?" Fourth, why it lands on an ordinary day.
It's easy to handle things for hours without meeting them: the phone, the door handle, the steering wheel, the mug. Ktaadn is Thoreau knocked out of that.
Not a vision of something beyond the world, but the world itself, suddenly undeniable, pressing back against him. Readers hear the passage differently: some hear terror, some awe, some both at once.
Thoreau doesn't settle it. He ends with questions, and leaves them open.

how: Some readers of The Maine Woods single out the Ktaadn passage, where Thoreau, descending the mountain, is overwhelmed by raw matter and cries out for contact; some take from it a practice of touching stone, bark or soil with full attention.

games.q: you're Thoreau, alone near the top of the mountain, and the cloud is so thick you can't see a thing. what do you do?
o: wait for days until it clears.
turn back, and find the moment on the way down.
write that the climb was wasted.
games.why: he turned back without a view. the passage people remember comes on the descent, on bare, burned-over ground.

practice: Feel the floor pushing back up through your heels, then put your hand on something solid, a tree, a brick wall, a wooden table, or flat on the floor, and press a little: the temperature, the grain, the weight that doesn't move for you.
Don't describe it. Once, quietly, ask Thoreau's questions without answering them: who are we? where are we? Then come back to your palm.

wordCard.voice: Contact on Ktaadn. Thoreau, coming down a Maine mountain, overwhelmed by plain matter: rocks, trees, wind. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: contact. The world isn't only around you; it presses back. Back tomorrow, same hill.
